[DAY2 18:20:01 - DAY2 18:20:28]
I touch my nose, continue walking, and reach my bedroom door. "The An and Ankang fish are collected," I say. I sit quietly and wave my hands as I watch Choiszt tune his guitar. I tilt my head and continue chatting with Choiszt. "20 minutes, 20 minutes down," I say. I see Nicous touch his hair. "That's fine," I say. "One more hour, right?" I say. I continue chatting with them.

[DAY2 18:20:30 - DAY2 18:20:59]
I tilt my head and chat with colleagues as I hear Choiszt playing the guitar. "I used one computer for 23 hours in one night," I say, then burst out laughing and feel very happy as I look toward my colleagues, who are each busy with their own affairs.

[DAY2 18:15:00 - DAY2 18:18:00]
I discussed the computer file transfer issue with Choiszt and Lucia, examining the process of copying documents by dragging them and noting that files appeared to disappear though the data remained on the hard drive. While observing Choiszt holding his guitar and picking up a mineral water bottle, I engaged in conversation about the transfer status, confirming with Choiszt that the data was still present but had not successfully transferred. We acknowledged potential technical limitations, such as the computer card not crashing, and set a task deadline, aiming to finish the work by 10 or 12, with plans for shooting until about 10:30 before moving on to other activities.

In the discussion about workflow and crew roles, I highlighted the need for a script supervisor to maintain a timeline and mark the plan accurately, emphasizing the importance of having someone dedicated to recording specific details like timing. I explained this by gesturing and giving examples of time tracking, suggesting that the script supervisor (S R) could start this process that night and iterate as needed. Throughout, I guided Choiszt in operating the computer, answering questions, and clarifying the "first perspective" approach for the project.

After standing up and moving a chair into the living room, I observed Choiszt playing guitar and reflected on the importance of having a continuous observer for scenes and locations, noting that individuals often cannot remember exact times themselves. I referenced the difficulties experienced on the first day compared to the smoother progress on the second day, concluding that having one person consistently follow along was sufficient for keeping track of the shoot’s timeline and details.
